name: Mopan
summary: A Mayan language of the Yucatecan branch, sister to Itza' and Yucatec Maya, spoken in San Luis, Petén, and in southern Belize. Also written Mopán or Mopan Maya.

conjugator.label: Verb
conjugator.hint: Type the verb as in the dictionary: emel «go down», janal «eat», jittal «lie down», ilik «see it».

own.hint: Type any verb and its meaning in English. If we don't detect it right, choose its type.
own.label: Verb
own.types_help: Transitive verbs end in -ik (käxtik «look for it»); write their meaning with «it». Positionals end in -tal. Root verbs end in a vowel + l repeating the vowel (emel, okol); activity verbs (janal, meyaj, tz'iib') make their past with uch.

source.full: Charles Andrew Hofling with Narcizo Asij, Ofelia Asis Cajbon and others, Mopan Maya–Spanish–English Dictionary (University of Utah Press, 2011); Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala, Muuch' t'an mopan: vocabulario mopan (2003). See also: Diccionario bilingüe maya mopán y español.

about: Mopan is a Mayan language of the Yucatecan branch, together with Yucatec Maya, Itza' and Lacandon. It is spoken in San Luis and other communities of southern Petén, in Guatemala, and in the Toledo District, in Belize.
The Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala recognizes it as one of the country's 21 Mayan language communities. In Belize it lives alongside Q'eqchi', English and Kriol.
Unlike Yucatec Maya, Mopan has no tones. It has a sixth vowel, ä, and writes the person joined to the verb: inwilaj «I saw it», tan intal «I am coming».

orthography.intro: We use the alphabet of the Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala: 6 vowels, which can be short or long, and plain or glottalized consonants. The apostrophe (') marks a glottalized consonant (k', t') or a glottal stop, a short break in the voice.
notes: Vowel length changes the meaning: kok «gravel», kook «deaf»; mis «cat», miis «broom».
B' and d' are implosive: air flows in as you say them. The other glottalized consonants (ch', k', p', t', tz') push it out.
R, f, g and d' appear almost only in loanwords and a few words.
Pronunciation is shown in brackets with the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA).

grammar.intro: A Mopan verb is built with an aspect marker, the pronoun joined to the verb and, in transitive verbs, a status suffix: -ik while it happens, -aj once it happened.

items.description: walak habit, tan going on, yan has to, ka' «that…».
in-, a-, u-, ti- joined to the verb; before a vowel inw-, aw-, uy-, tiw-.

blocks.title: Two sets of pronouns
blocks.description: Set A goes joined before the verb: who does the action. Set B goes at the end: the object, and the subject of intransitive verbs in the past and the subjunctive.
blocks.note: «We» with -e'ex at the end includes the listener: tiwemele'ex «we all go down».

blocks.title: Three ways of saying «it happened»
blocks.description: In the completive, each type of intransitive verb marks the person in its own way.

items.name: Root verbs
items.description: Verbs in vowel + l repeating the vowel, and tal, b'eel: the root and set B.

items.name: Activity verbs
items.description: Verbs like janal, meyaj, tz'iib': uchi «it happened» + the verb with its pronoun.

items.name: Positionals
items.description: Verbs in -tal that say how the body ends up.

blocks.title: Transitive verbs
blocks.description: The transitive completive takes no aspect prefix. In the subjunctive and the imperative, root verbs end in a vowel echoing the root's; -t- verbs, in -e.

blocks.title: Negation and orders
blocks.description: Ma' negates; with the ongoing aspect it becomes ma' t-. To forbid, ma' goes with the 2nd-person pronoun.

tenses.name: Completive
tenses.description: What already happened: set B in root verbs, uch in activity verbs, -aj in transitive verbs.

tenses.name: Subjunctive
tenses.description: «That…»: what isn't real yet (ka' + dependent status).

lexicon.note: Irregular: past b'ini, subjunctive xi'ik, imperative xen
